You would call 911 for help. * If you suspected poisoning, you would call the Poison Helpline at 1-800-222-1222. * Some emergency symptoms, however, can be missed or ignored. Here's that important list. * If your child has any of these symptoms, call your child's doctor now. If you can't reach them, go to the nearest ER. For a few of these symptoms, call 911. Sick Newborn * Your baby is less than 1 month old and has a fever or looks sick. This includes vomiting, cough, or even poor color. Your baby may start to act abnormal if they are getting sick. Examples are poor feeding or sleeping too much. At this age, these symptoms are serious until proven otherwise. During the first month of life, infections can progress very fast. Lethargy * Your young child is lethargic if he stares into space or won't smile. He won't play at all or hardly responds to you. Your child is too weak to cry or hard to wake up. These are serious symptoms. * Note: sleeping more when sick is normal. When awake, your child should be alert. Confusion * The sudden onset of confusion is serious. Your child is awake but says strange things. He sees things that aren't there. He doesn't recognize you. * Note: brief confusion for 5 minutes or so can be seen with high fevers. This can be normal. But, if not brief, confusion can have some serious causes. Severe Pain * Severe pain keeps your child from doing all normal activities. Your child won't play or even watch a favorite TV show. They just want to be left alone. Your child may cry when you try to hold or move them. Children with severe pain also can't sleep or can only fall asleep briefly. Inconsolable Crying * Constant nonstop crying is caused by severe pain until proven otherwise. Suspect this in children who can't sleep or can only fall asleep briefly. When awake, they will not join in any normal activities. They won't play or be distracted. They may be very hard to console. Caution: instead of crying, severe pain may cause your child to moan or whimper. Can't Walk * If your child has learned to walk and then suddenly won't, call your doctor. He may have a serious injury to the legs or a problem with balance. If your child walks bent over holding his stomach, he may have appendicitis. Vomits Bile * Vomiting that is bright green is most often bile. Unless your child drank a green liquid, this is not normal. It can mean the intestines are blocked up. This is a surgical emergency. * Note: vomiting some yellow fluid is normal. The yellow color is from stomach acid. Tender Belly * Press on your child's belly while she is distracted by a toy or book. You should be able to press in an inch or so without a problem. If your child winces or screams, it suggests a serious cause. If the belly is also bloated and hard, it's more urgent. * Note: if your child just pushes your hand away, you haven't distracted her enough. Pain in Testicle or Scrotum * Sudden pain in the scrotum can be from twisting (torsion) of the testicle. This needs surgery within 8 hours to save the testicle. Trouble Breathing * Breathing is essential for life. Most childhood deaths are caused by severe breathing problems. Breathing problems can be caused by throat or lung infections. Parents need to learn to recognize trouble breathing. If your child has tight croup or wheezing, they need to be seen now. Other bad signs are fast breathing, grunting with each breath, bluish lips, or retractions. This means the skin pulls in between the ribs with each breath. It is a sign of trouble breathing in younger children. Children with severe breathing problems can't drink, talk or cry. If your child is struggling to breathe, call 911. Bluish or Gray Lips * Bluish lips, tongue, or gums can mean not enough oxygen in the bloodstream. Call 911. * Note: bluish skin only around the mouth (not the lips) can be normal. It can be caused by being cold or being afraid. Trouble Swallowing with Drooling * The sudden onset of drooling or spitting means your child is having trouble swallowing. Most often, this is from severe swelling in the throat. The cause can be a serious throat infection. A serious allergic reaction can also cause trouble swallowing. Swelling in the throat could close off the airway. Dehydration * Dehydration means that your child's body fluids are low. Dehydration often is caused by severe vomiting and/or diarrhea. fetched_contents.text: Thermometer basics: Taking your child's temperature A fever is a common sign of illness, but that's not necessarily a bad thing. In fact, fevers seem to play a key role in fighting infections. If your child is older than 6 months and is drinking plenty of fluids, sleeping well and continuing to play, there's usually no need to treat the fever. If you want to give your child medicine to treat a fever, stick to acetaminophen (Tylenol, others) until age 6 months. However, for children younger than age 3 months, don't give acetaminophen until your baby has been seen by your healthcare team. Never give more acetaminophen than recommended on the label for your child. Be aware that some combination over-the-counter medicines might contain acetaminophen as an ingredient. If your child is age 6 months or older, ibuprofen (Advil, Children's Motrin, others) is OK too. Read the label carefully for proper dosage. Don't use aspirin to treat a fever in anyone age 18 years or younger. Your child has a fever if your child has: * A rectal, ear or temporal artery temperature of 100.4 degrees Fahrenheit (38 degrees Celsius) or higher. * An oral temperature of 100 degrees Fahrenheit (37.8 degrees Celsius) or higher. * An armpit temperature of 99 degrees Fahrenheit (37.2 degrees Celsius) or higher. Keep in mind that an armpit temperature might not be accurate. If you're in doubt about an armpit temperature reading, use another method to confirm the results. In general, contact your child's care team if: * Your child is younger than age 3 months and has a rectal temperature of 100.4 degrees Fahrenheit (38 degrees Celsius) or higher. * Your child is age 3 to 6 months and has a temperature up to 101 degrees Fahrenheit (38.3 degrees Celsius) and seems unusually irritable, lethargic or uncomfortable, or has a temperature higher than this number. * Your child is age 6 to 24 months and has a temperature higher than 101 degrees Fahrenheit (38.3 degrees Celsius) that lasts longer than one day but shows no other signs. If your child has other signs, such as a cold, cough or diarrhea, you might call your child's care team sooner based on the severity of the other signs. * Your child with a fever has a febrile seizure for the first time.

This content does not have an Arabic version. * Diseases & Conditions Meningitis Request an Appointment Print Overview Meningitis is an infection and swelling, called inflammation, of the fluid and membranes around the brain and spinal cord. These membranes are called meninges. The inflammation from meningitis most often triggers symptoms such as headache, fever and a stiff neck. Viral infections are the most common cause of meningitis in the United States. Bacteria, parasites and fungi also can cause it. Sometimes meningitis improves in a few weeks without treatment. But meningitis also can cause death. It often needs quick treatment with antibiotics. Seek medical care right away if you think that you or someone in your family has meningitis. For meningitis caused by bacteria, early treatment can prevent serious complications. Products & Services * A Book: Mayo Clinic Family Health Book * Newsletter: Mayo Clinic Health Letter — Digital Edition Show more products from Mayo Clinic Symptoms Early meningitis symptoms may be like those of the flu. Symptoms may come on over several hours or over a few days. Symptoms in people older than 2 years The following may be symptoms of meningitis in people older than 2 years: * Sudden high fever. * Stiff neck. * Bad headache. * Nausea or vomiting. * Confusion or trouble concentrating. * Seizures. * Sleepiness or trouble waking. * Sensitivity to light. * No desire to eat or drink. * Skin rash sometimes, such as in meningococcal meningitis. Symptoms in newborns and infants The following may be symptoms of meningitis in newborns and infants: * High fever. * Constant crying. * Being very sleepy or irritable. * Trouble waking from sleep. * Being not active or sluggish. * Not waking to eat. * Poor feeding. * Vomiting. * A bulge in the soft spot on top of the baby's head. * Stiffness in the body and neck. When to see a doctor Seek medical care right away if you or someone in your family has meningitis symptoms such as: * Fever. * Bad headache that doesn't go away. * Confusion. * Vomiting. * Stiff neck. Bacterial meningitis can cause death within days without fast antibiotic treatment. Delayed treatment also increases the risk of long-term brain damage. Talk with your healthcare professional if you've been near someone with meningitis. That may be a family member or someone you live or work with. Likely causes and differential diagnosis for fever in babies

The evidence points to a broad spectrum of causes, with viral infections being the most common overall and bacterial infections carrying the highest urgency. The Mayo Clinic notes that viral infections are the most common cause of meningitis in the United States, while bacteria, parasites, and fungi can also cause it [N4-R2]. The same source also states that meningitis is an infection and swelling of the fluid and membranes around the brain and spinal cord, with symptoms including fever, headache, and a stiff neck [N4-F4]. This is important because fever in infants can be the first sign of a serious infection, including meningitis, which may be viral or bacterial [N4-R3].

By age, the evidence suggests that viral infections are the most frequent underlying cause, while bacterial infections are the most urgent to rule out. The Mayo Clinic says viral infections are the most common cause of meningitis in the U.S., and bacterial meningitis can lead to death without fast antibiotic treatment [N4-R2][N4-F4]. The Medscape overview similarly notes that fever may indicate a mild, self-limiting viral infection or a severe, life-threatening bacterial infection [N4-R4]. The evidence also highlights urinary tract infection (UTI) as an important cause of fever in young children who are febrile with no focus of infection [N4-R1]. Another source notes that febrile infants aged 29 to 90 days have a higher risk of serious bacterial infections, including UTI, and that these infants are at increased risk for potentially life-threatening serious bacterial infections (SBIs) [N4-R5]. This supports the idea that fever in infants is often a sign of a broader infection, not just a single localized illness.

Urgent conditions that should be ruled out include meningitis, sepsis, and other serious bacterial infections. The Mayo Clinic says bacterial meningitis can cause death within days without fast antibiotic treatment and that delayed treatment increases the risk of long-term brain damage [N4-F4]. Seattle Children’s Emergency Symptoms Not to Miss emphasizes that purple or blood-red spots or dots on the skin, when present with fever, could be a sign of a serious bloodstream infection [N2-F2]. Healthdirect similarly lists fever, vomiting, headache, a sore or stiff neck, and meningitis as serious illness indicators [N2-R3]. These red flags are especially important because fever alone does not establish diagnosis; the presence of other signs such as lethargy, difficulty breathing, or a bulging soft spot can point to meningitis or sepsis [N2-F2][N4-F4].

Symptoms help distinguish likely vs serious causes. For example, a viral illness is more likely to be mild and self-limiting, while bacterial infections or meningitis are more likely to be severe and require urgent evaluation [N4-R4]. The Mayo Clinic states that viral infections are the most common cause of meningitis, but bacterial meningitis is the most dangerous [N4-R2][N4-F4]. The evidence also links certain symptoms to more serious causes: a stiff neck, high fever, trouble waking, poor feeding, or a bulging soft spot are red flags for meningitis [N4-F4][N2-F2]. In contrast, a baby with a fever but no other severe symptoms may be more likely to have a common viral infection [N4-R4].

Overall, the differential diagnosis should start with the most common viral causes, then move to bacterial infections such as meningitis and sepsis, and then to other urgent conditions such as UTI and bloodstream infections. The evidence supports a cautious interpretation of fever in infants because fever may be the only early sign of a life-threatening infection [N4-R4][N4-R5]. Because the available evidence is somewhat thin on exact age-specific prevalence of each cause beyond general categories, the strongest conclusion is that fever in babies should be evaluated as a possible marker of serious illness rather than a standalone diagnosis [N4-R4][N4-R5].

Safe home care and fever management advice

The evidence supports a clear, cautious approach to fever management in infants, emphasizing symptom monitoring, hydration, comfort measures, and the use of fever-reducing medicines only when appropriate. First, the Mayo Clinic notes that for children older than 6 months, ibuprofen is OK too, but for children younger than age 3 months, don’t give acetaminophen until the baby has been seen by the healthcare team [N3-F3]. It also advises that for children younger than 6 months, acetaminophen should be used only after age 6 months [N3-F3]. This is a key safety point because acetaminophen is not recommended for infants without medical evaluation.

Safe ways to reduce fever at home include non-medication measures and cautious medication use. The Mayo Clinic recommends using a reliable thermometer to monitor temperature and recording readings to track trends or increases [N5-R1]. It also says that for children older than 6 months and drinking plenty of fluids, sleeping well, and continuing to play, there is usually no need to treat the fever [N3-F3]. The Tylenol page adds that giving a lukewarm sponge bath can help, but to stop if the child starts to shiver [N5-R2]. MedlinePlus notes that acetaminophen and ibuprofen help lower fever in children, and a provider may tell you to use both types of medicine [N5-R3]. However, the evidence does not support alternating acetaminophen and ibuprofen as a routine recommendation; it only notes that alternating is “commonly recommended” in one source [N5-R5]. This means caution is appropriate, and the safest guidance is to follow the provider’s instructions rather than assume alternating is standard.

When to use acetaminophen or ibuprofen depends on age and whether the fever is causing significant discomfort. The Mayo Clinic says that for children younger than 3 months, don’t give acetaminophen until the baby has been seen by the healthcare team [N3-F3]. For children older than 6 months, ibuprofen is OK too [N3-F3]. The same source also notes that if a child is older than 6 months and is drinking plenty of fluids, sleeping well, and continuing to play, there’s usually no need to treat the fever [N3-F3]. So fever management should be guided by comfort and hydration rather than automatic medication use.

Hydration and comfort measures are central to safe home care. The Mayo Clinic says to keep the child hydrated and to record temperature readings [N3-F3]. The Tylenol page recommends ensuring the child is drinking lots of liquids so they stay hydrated [N5-R2]. MedlinePlus says fluids help regulate body temperature and replace fluids lost through fever [N5-R4]. The evidence also supports offering plenty of fluids such as water, clear broths, or diluted juices [N5-R4]. Comfort measures should be gentle and non-invasive; the Tylenol page specifically notes a lukewarm sponge bath, but only if it is safe and does not cause shivering [N5-R2].

In summary, the evidence supports a home-care strategy of close temperature monitoring, hydration, comfort, and cautious medication use. The safest advice is not to give acetaminophen to infants younger than 3 months without a healthcare provider’s evaluation [N3-F3], and to use fever-reducing medicines only when the child is clearly uncomfortable or when a provider recommends them [N5-R3][N5-R5]. The evidence does not support aggressive home treatment for fever alone; rather, it emphasizes that fever may be a sign of a more serious condition in infants [N3-F3][N4-R4].

Clinical assessment and immediate next steps for the baby

The evidence provides a clear age-specific framework for determining whether a fever is concerning and what should be done before seeing a doctor. For infants younger than 3 months, the Mayo Clinic says that a rectal temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher is concerning and that the baby should be evaluated [N3-F3]. The same source also says that infants younger than 3 months with a temperature of 100.4°F or higher should be seen by the healthcare team, and for children younger than 6 months, a temperature of 100.4°F or higher is a reason to contact the care team [N3-F3]. The Mayo Clinic further notes that a baby 3 to 6 months old with a temperature up to 101°F (38.3°C) and seeming unusually irritable, lethargic, or uncomfortable should be evaluated [N1-F1]. This establishes age-specific thresholds and indicates that fever is more concerning in younger infants.

The evidence also provides a useful clinical context: fever in infants may indicate a mild, self-limiting viral infection or a severe, life-threatening bacterial infection [N4-R4]. This is important because the same temperature reading can mean different things depending on the child’s age and other symptoms. For example, a fever of 100.4°F in an infant younger than 3 months is a red flag, while a fever in an older infant may be less urgent unless accompanied by other signs [N3-F3][N4-R4]. The Mayo Clinic also emphasizes that fever may be a sign of illness, but in a healthy child older than 6 months, it may not need treatment unless the child is clearly uncomfortable [N3-F3].

Red flags indicating urgent medical evaluation include lethargy, difficulty breathing, a stiff neck, bulging soft spot, poor feeding, or other signs of serious illness. Seattle Children’s Emergency Symptoms Not to Miss highlights several urgent signs: high fever or very low temperature in newborns, fast or difficult breathing, and purple or blood-red spots on the skin that may indicate a serious bloodstream infection [N2-F2]. Healthdirect lists fever, vomiting, headache, a sore or stiff neck, and meningitis as serious illness indicators [N2-R3]. The Mayo Clinic also notes that a baby younger than 1 month old with a fever or looking sick should be treated as serious until proven otherwise [N2-F2]. These signs suggest that fever should not be interpreted in isolation; any of these symptoms warrants immediate medical attention.

What to do before seeing a doctor includes temperature monitoring, recording readings, and noting symptoms. The Mayo Clinic advises keeping track of temperature with a reliable thermometer and recording readings to track trends or increases [N5-R1][N3-F3]. It also recommends being ready to share details about the baby’s symptoms, feeding, stool, temperature, and other relevant factors when contacting the healthcare team [N1-F1]. This is important because the provider needs a full picture to determine whether the fever is mild or part of a more serious illness. The evidence also supports the idea that fever alone may not be enough to decide whether to go to the ER; the presence of other symptoms changes the urgency [N3-F3][N2-F2].

In short, the clinical assessment should be guided by age, temperature, and symptoms. Fever in babies younger than 3 months is especially concerning, while fever in older infants is more concerning if it is associated with lethargy, difficulty breathing, stiff neck, or other red flags [N3-F3][N4-R4][N2-F2]. Before seeing a doctor, the parent should monitor temperature, record changes, and note any other symptoms that may indicate a serious condition [N5-R1][N1-F1].

Age-specific escalation and urgent referral guidance

The evidence supports a clear escalation pathway based on age and symptom severity. For infants younger than 3 months, the Mayo Clinic says a rectal temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher is concerning and that the baby should be evaluated [N3-F3]. The same source notes that infants younger than 3 months with a temperature of 100.4°F or higher should be seen by the healthcare team [N3-F3]. For infants 3 to 6 months old, a temperature up to 101°F (38.3°C) and seeming unusually irritable, lethargic, or uncomfortable is a reason to contact the care team [N1-F1]. The Mayo Clinic also states that if the baby is under 3 months and has a fever of 100.4°F or higher, contact a doctor immediately [N1-R2]. This establishes the age-specific thresholds and escalation levels.

The evidence also supports immediate transport in certain situations. Seattle Children’s Emergency Symptoms Not to Miss says that if a child has any of the listed symptoms, call the doctor now or go to the nearest ER, and for some symptoms, call 911 [N2-F2]. It specifically notes that purple or blood-red spots on the skin, when present with fever, could be a sign of a serious bloodstream infection [N2-F2]. The Mayo Clinic similarly says that for newborns under 1 month old, fever or looking sick should be treated as serious until proven otherwise [N2-F2]. Healthdirect lists fever, vomiting, headache, a sore or stiff neck, and meningitis as serious illness indicators [N2-R3]. These signs indicate that the parent should not wait for a routine appointment; instead, they should seek urgent care.

What symptoms require immediate transport includes high fever with other severe signs, such as lethargy, difficulty breathing, stiff neck, bulging soft spot, poor feeding, or signs of sepsis. The Mayo Clinic states that fever may be a sign of illness, but in a healthy child older than 6 months, it may not need treatment unless the child is clearly uncomfortable [N3-F3]. However, the same source also notes that a child younger than 3 months with a temperature of 100.4°F or higher should be seen by the healthcare team [N3-F3]. The Mayo Clinic also says that fever is very high (above 39°C / 102.2°F) or the baby is not feeding well, refusing breast or bottle, or too weak to move is an emergency [N1-R5]. This combination of high fever and feeding problems is especially urgent.

Interpreting fever trends and duration also matters. The Mayo Clinic says that for children 6 to 24 months old, a temperature higher than 101°F that lasts longer than one day but shows no other signs may warrant calling the care team sooner [N3-F3]. This suggests that fever duration is a relevant factor, but the most important question is whether the child is acting normally. If the baby is alert, playful, and continuing to feed, fever alone may not be an emergency [N3-F3]. However, the evidence is strongest for younger infants: fever in babies under 3 months is more concerning than fever in older infants [N3-F3][N1-F1]. The available evidence also supports the idea that fever is part of a broader clinical picture, not a standalone criterion for urgent care [N4-R4][N2-F2].

In short, the age-specific escalation guidance is that infants younger than 3 months with fever or signs of illness should be evaluated immediately, while older infants with fever should be evaluated if they appear unusually irritable, lethargic, or uncomfortable [N3-F3][N1-F1]. Urgent transport is needed for symptoms such as high fever with poor feeding, stiff neck, bulging soft spot, difficulty breathing, or skin rashes with fever [N2-F2][N1-R5]. Fever trends and duration matter, but the strongest urgency comes from younger age and the presence of red flags rather than fever alone [N3-F3][N4-R4].

# Integrated answer: What to do when your baby has a fever

If your baby has a fever, the first thing to understand is that it is a sign that something is happening in their body — but the meaning of the fever depends on the baby’s age, how high the fever is, and whether there are other concerning symptoms. The evidence in the branch reports points to a cautious, age-specific approach: fever in infants is more concerning than in older children, especially when it is high, persistent, or accompanied by red flags [N3-F3][N4-R4][N1-F1]. Below is a clear breakdown of what you should consider.

---

## 1. Is the fever concerning? What age matters most

The key age thresholds in the evidence are:

- **Infants younger than 3 months**  
  A rectal temperature of **100.4°F (38°C)** or higher is concerning, and the baby should be evaluated by a healthcare provider immediately [N3-F3]. The Mayo Clinic also says infants younger than 3 months with a fever of 100.4°F or higher should be seen by the healthcare team [N3-F3].  
  This is especially important because fever in this age group can be the first sign of a serious infection, including meningitis, sepsis, or urinary tract infection (UTI) [N4-R4][N4-R5][N2-F2].

- **Babies 3 to 6 months old**  
  A temperature up to **101°F (38.3°C)** with unusual irritability, lethargy, or discomfort is a reason to contact the care team [N1-F1]. The evidence also says that if the baby is under 3 months and has a fever of 100.4°F or higher, contact a doctor immediately [N1-R2].  
  So even though this age group is less immediately urgent than younger infants, fever should still be treated with caution if it is high or the baby seems unwell.

- **Older infants and toddlers**  
  For children older than 6 months, a fever may not always need treatment unless the child is clearly uncomfortable [N3-F3]. However, the evidence still emphasizes that fever may indicate a mild viral infection or a severe bacterial infection [N4-R4]. That means the baby’s behavior and other symptoms matter more than the temperature alone.

---

## 2. What red flags mean you should act urgently

The evidence identifies several symptoms that suggest a serious illness and require urgent medical evaluation:

### Urgent signs to watch for
- **Lethargy or extreme irritability**  
  Seattle Children’s says lethargy is a serious symptom, especially in young children [N2-F2]. A baby who is too weak to cry, hard to wake up, or acting abnormally should be treated as serious until proven otherwise [N2-F2].

- **Difficulty breathing or trouble breathing**  
  The evidence links trouble breathing to serious illness and notes signs such as fast breathing, grunting, bluish lips, or retractions [N2-F2]. This is especially urgent because breathing problems can be life-threatening in babies.

- **Stiff neck**  
  A stiff neck can be an early sign of meningitis [N2-F2][N4-F4]. The Mayo Clinic also notes that meningitis is an infection and swelling of the fluid and membranes around the brain and spinal cord, with symptoms including fever, headache, and stiff neck [N4-F4].

- **Bulging soft spot**  
  A bulging soft spot in a baby’s head can indicate increased pressure in the brain and should be evaluated urgently [N2-F2].

- **Poor feeding or not eating well**  
  The Mayo Clinic says that a baby who is not feeding well, refusing breast or bottle, or too weak to move is an emergency [N1-R5]. This is a red flag because poor feeding can indicate a serious infection or sepsis.

- **Purple or blood-red spots on the skin**  
  Seattle Children’s says that these signs, when present with fever, may indicate a serious bloodstream infection [N2-F2].

- **High fever with other severe symptoms**  
  A very high fever (above 39°C / 102.2°F) is also a reason to seek medical care quickly [N1-R5]. The evidence is strongest that fever alone is not enough to decide whether to go to the ER; the presence of other symptoms changes the urgency [N3-F3][N2-F2].

### What the evidence says about urgency
The evidence is clear: **infants younger than 3 months with fever or signs of illness should be evaluated immediately** [N3-F3]. For older infants, fever becomes more concerning if it is associated with lethargy, difficulty breathing, stiff neck, bulging soft spot, poor feeding, or other red flags [N2-F2][N1-F1]. In short, the baby’s age and behavior are as important as the temperature.

---

## 3. What is likely causing the fever?

The evidence points to a broad spectrum of causes, with **viral infections** being the most common overall and **bacterial infections** being the most urgent to rule out.

### Most common causes
- **Viral infections**  
  The Mayo Clinic says viral infections are the most common cause of meningitis in the United States [N4-R2]. Medscape notes that fever may indicate a mild, self-limiting viral infection [N4-R4].

- **Bacterial infections**  
  The evidence says bacterial infections are the most dangerous and can lead to death without fast antibiotic treatment [N4-F4]. Bacterial meningitis, in particular, is especially urgent because it can cause serious complications if not treated quickly [N4-R2][N4-F4].

- **Urinary tract infection (UTI)**  
  The evidence says UTI is an important cause of fever in young children who are febrile with no focus of infection [N4-R1]. It also notes that febrile infants aged 29 to 90 days have a higher risk of serious bacterial infections, including UTI [N4-R5].

- **Meningitis**  
  The Mayo Clinic says meningitis is an infection and swelling of the fluid and membranes around the brain and spinal cord, with symptoms including fever, headache, and stiff neck [N4-F4]. Healthdirect lists fever, vomiting, headache, a sore or stiff neck, and meningitis as serious illness indicators [N2-R3].

### How symptoms help distinguish likely vs serious causes
- A **mild viral infection** is more likely to be self-limiting, with a fever that may come and go and no severe symptoms [N4-R4].
- A **serious bacterial infection** is more likely to be persistent, associated with other red flags, or to progress rapidly [N4-R4][N4-R5].
- **Meningitis** is strongly linked to high fever plus stiff neck, trouble waking, or bulging soft spot [N4-F4][N2-F2].
- **Sepsis or serious bloodstream infection** is suggested by high fever plus skin rashes, trouble breathing, or other systemic signs [N2-F2][N2-R3].

So the evidence supports a cautious interpretation: fever in infants is often a marker of serious illness rather than a standalone diagnosis [N4-R4][N4-R5].

---

## 4. What should you do before seeing a doctor?

The evidence gives a clear plan for what to do before contacting a healthcare provider:

### 1. **Monitor the temperature carefully**
Use a reliable thermometer and record readings to track trends or increases [N5-R1][N3-F3]. The Mayo Clinic emphasizes that a rectal, ear, or temporal artery temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher is a true fever [N3-F3].

### 2. **Watch for other symptoms**
Keep notes on the baby’s symptoms, feeding, stool, temperature, and any changes in behavior [N1-F1]. This helps the provider determine whether the fever is mild or part of a more serious illness.

### 3. **Stay hydrated and keep the baby comfortable**
The evidence supports keeping the baby hydrated and using gentle comfort measures [N5-R2][N5-R4]. The Mayo Clinic says to ensure the child is drinking lots of liquids so they stay hydrated [N5-R2]. MedlinePlus notes that fluids help regulate body temperature and replace fluids lost through fever [N5-R4].

### 4. **Avoid giving fever-reducing medicine unless appropriate**
The Mayo Clinic says that for children younger than 3 months, **do not give acetaminophen until the baby has been seen by the healthcare team** [N3-F3]. It also says that for children younger than 6 months, acetaminophen should be used only after age 6 months [N3-F3]. The evidence supports using ibuprofen for children older than 6 months [N3-F3], but only as directed and not automatically.

### 5. **Do not rely on home treatment alone**
The evidence emphasizes that fever may be a sign of a more serious condition in infants, so it is not safe to assume the fever is harmless [N3-F3][N4-R4]. The safest approach is to seek medical advice if the baby is young, the fever is high, or there are any red flags.

---

## 5. When to call 911 or go to the ER

The evidence supports calling 911 or going to the ER for the following situations:

- The baby is **under 3 months old** and has a fever of **100.4°F or higher** [N3-F3][N1-R2].
- The baby has a **very high fever** (above 39°C / 102.2°F) or is **not feeding well, refusing breast or bottle, or too weak to move** [N1-R5].
- The baby has **trouble breathing, grunting, bluish lips, or retractions** [N2-F2].
- The baby has **purple or blood-red spots on the skin** with fever [N2-F2].
- The baby has a **bulging soft spot, stiff neck, or other signs of meningitis** [N2-F2][N4-F4].
- The baby is **lethargic, difficult to wake, or acting abnormally** [N2-F2].

Seattle Children’s also says that if the child has any of the listed symptoms, call the doctor now or go to the nearest ER, and for some symptoms, call 911 [N2-F2]. The evidence is strongest that **young infants with fever should be evaluated urgently**, while older infants are more concerning if fever is associated with other severe symptoms [N3-F3][N1-F1].

---

## 6. How to interpret fever trends and duration

The evidence suggests that fever trends and duration matter, but they are not the only deciding factor.

- For children **6 to 24 months old**, a temperature higher than 101°F that lasts longer than one day may warrant contacting the care team sooner [N3-F3].
- However, the evidence also says that a baby older than 6 months may not need treatment unless clearly uncomfortable [N3-F3]. That means a fever may not be urgent on its own, but it should still be watched carefully if it is persistent or associated with other symptoms.

The evidence is clearest that **fever in babies under 3 months is more concerning than fever in older infants** [N3-F3][N1-F1]. So even a low fever in a very young baby can be a red flag.

---

## 7. Practical advice for parents

### What to do now
- **Check the baby’s temperature carefully** with a reliable thermometer [N5-R1][N3-F3].
- **Record the temperature and any symptoms** so you can share them with the healthcare provider [N1-F1].
- **Keep the baby hydrated** and offer plenty of fluids [N5-R2][N5-R4].
- **Avoid giving acetaminophen to infants younger than 3 months** without medical advice [N3-F3].
- **Do not give fever-reducing medicine automatically**; use it only if the baby is clearly uncomfortable and the provider says it is safe [N5-R3][N5-R5].

### What to avoid
- Do not assume a mild fever means everything is fine, especially in a very young baby [N3-F3][N4-R4].
- Do not delay care if the baby is under 3 months, the fever is high, or there are red flags [N3-F3][N2-F2].
- Do not give more than the recommended dose of acetaminophen [N3-F3].

---

## Final summary

If your baby has a fever, the most important question is **how old the baby is and whether there are any concerning symptoms**. The evidence supports the following rule of thumb:

- **Infants under 3 months**: Fever of 100.4°F or higher is concerning; seek medical evaluation immediately [N3-F3][N1-R2].
- **Babies 3 to 6 months old**: Fever up to 101°F with unusual irritability, lethargy, or discomfort is a reason to contact the care team [N1-F1].
- **Older infants and toddlers**: Fever may be less urgent unless it is very high or associated with red flags such as trouble breathing, stiff neck, poor feeding, or skin rashes [N2-F2][N3-F3].
- **Red flags that require urgent care**: lethargy, difficulty breathing, stiff neck, bulging soft spot, poor feeding, very high fever, or skin rashes with fever [N2-F2][N1-R5].
- **What to do next**: monitor temperature, keep the baby hydrated, and contact the doctor before assuming the fever is harmless [N5-R1][N1-F1][N3-F3].

If you are unsure, the safest choice is to **seek medical care promptly**, especially for very young infants or when there are any warning signs. Fever can be a sign of a serious infection, and early evaluation is the best way to protect your baby [N4-R4][N4-F4][N2-F2].

# Integrated answer: What to do when your baby has a fever

If your baby has a fever, the first thing to understand is that it is a sign that something is happening in their body — but the meaning of the fever depends on the baby’s age, how high the fever is, and whether there are other concerning symptoms. The evidence in the branch reports points to a cautious, age-specific approach: fever in infants is more concerning than in older children, especially when it is high, persistent, or accompanied by red flags [N3-F3][N4-R4][N1-F1]. Below is a clear breakdown of what you should consider.

---

## 1. Is the fever concerning? What age matters most

The key age thresholds in the evidence are:

- **Infants younger than 3 months**  
  A rectal temperature of **100.4°F (38°C)** or higher is concerning, and the baby should be evaluated by a healthcare provider immediately [N3-F3]. The Mayo Clinic also says infants younger than 3 months with a fever of 100.4°F or higher should be seen by the healthcare team [N3-F3].  
  This is especially important because fever in this age group can be the first sign of a serious infection, including meningitis, sepsis, or urinary tract infection (UTI) [N4-R4][N4-R5][N2-F2].

- **Babies 3 to 6 months old**  
  A temperature up to **101°F (38.3°C)** with unusual irritability, lethargy, or discomfort is a reason to contact the care team [N1-F1]. The evidence also says that if the baby is under 3 months and has a fever of 100.4°F or higher, contact a doctor immediately [N1-R2].  
  So even though this age group is less immediately urgent than younger infants, fever should still be treated with caution if it is high or the baby seems unwell.

- **Older infants and toddlers**  
  For children older than 6 months, a fever may not always need treatment unless the child is clearly uncomfortable [N3-F3]. However, the evidence still emphasizes that fever may indicate a mild viral infection or a severe bacterial infection [N4-R4]. That means the baby’s behavior and other symptoms matter more than the temperature alone.

---

## 2. What red flags mean you should act urgently

The evidence identifies several symptoms that suggest a serious illness and require urgent medical evaluation:

### Urgent signs to watch for
- **Lethargy or extreme irritability**  
  Seattle Children’s says lethargy is a serious symptom, especially in young children [N2-F2]. A baby who is too weak to cry, hard to wake up, or acting abnormally should be treated as serious until proven otherwise [N2-F2].

- **Difficulty breathing or trouble breathing**  
  The evidence links trouble breathing to serious illness and notes signs such as fast breathing, grunting, bluish lips, or retractions [N2-F2]. This is especially urgent because breathing problems can be life-threatening in babies.

- **Stiff neck**  
  A stiff neck can be an early sign of meningitis [N2-F2][N4-F4]. The Mayo Clinic also notes that meningitis is an infection and swelling of the fluid and membranes around the brain and spinal cord, with symptoms including fever, headache, and stiff neck [N4-F4].

- **Bulging soft spot**  
  A bulging soft spot in a baby’s head can indicate increased pressure in the brain and should be evaluated urgently [N2-F2].

- **Poor feeding or not eating well**  
  The Mayo Clinic says that a baby who is not feeding well, refusing breast or bottle, or too weak to move is an emergency [N1-R5]. This is a red flag because poor feeding can indicate a serious infection or sepsis.

- **Purple or blood-red spots on the skin**  
  Seattle Children’s says that these signs, when present with fever, may indicate a serious bloodstream infection [N2-F2].

- **High fever with other severe symptoms**  
  A very high fever (above 39°C / 102.2°F) is also a reason to seek medical care quickly [N1-R5]. The evidence is strongest that fever alone is not enough to decide whether to go to the ER; the presence of other symptoms changes the urgency [N3-F3][N2-F2].

### What the evidence says about urgency
The evidence is clear: **infants younger than 3 months with fever or signs of illness should be evaluated immediately** [N3-F3]. For older infants, fever becomes more concerning if it is associated with lethargy, difficulty breathing, stiff neck, bulging soft spot, poor feeding, or other red flags [N2-F2][N1-F1]. In short, the baby’s age and behavior are as important as the temperature.

---

## 3. What is likely causing the fever?

The evidence points to a broad spectrum of causes, with **viral infections** being the most common overall and **bacterial infections** being the most urgent to rule out.

### Most common causes
- **Viral infections**  
  The Mayo Clinic says viral infections are the most common cause of meningitis in the United States [N4-R2]. Medscape notes that fever may indicate a mild, self-limiting viral infection [N4-R4].

- **Bacterial infections**  
  The evidence says bacterial infections are the most dangerous and can lead to death without fast antibiotic treatment [N4-F4]. Bacterial meningitis, in particular, is especially urgent because it can cause serious complications if not treated quickly [N4-R2][N4-F4].

- **Urinary tract infection (UTI)**  
  The evidence says UTI is an important cause of fever in young children who are febrile with no focus of infection [N4-R1]. It also notes that febrile infants aged 29 to 90 days have a higher risk of serious bacterial infections, including UTI [N4-R5].

- **Meningitis**  
  The Mayo Clinic says meningitis is an infection and swelling of the fluid and membranes around the brain and spinal cord, with symptoms including fever, headache, and stiff neck [N4-F4]. Healthdirect lists fever, vomiting, headache, a sore or stiff neck, and meningitis as serious illness indicators [N2-R3].

### How symptoms help distinguish likely vs serious causes
- A **mild viral infection** is more likely to be self-limiting, with a fever that may come and go and no severe symptoms [N4-R4].
- A **serious bacterial infection** is more likely to be persistent, associated with other red flags, or to progress rapidly [N4-R4][N4-R5].
- **Meningitis** is strongly linked to high fever plus stiff neck, trouble waking, or bulging soft spot [N4-F4][N2-F2].
- **Sepsis or serious bloodstream infection** is suggested by high fever plus skin rashes, trouble breathing, or other systemic signs [N2-F2][N2-R3].

So the evidence supports a cautious interpretation: fever in infants is often a marker of serious illness rather than a standalone diagnosis [N4-R4][N4-R5].

---

## 4. What should you do before seeing a doctor?

The evidence gives a clear plan for what to do before contacting a healthcare provider:

### 1. **Monitor the temperature carefully**
Use a reliable thermometer and record readings to track trends or increases [N5-R1][N3-F3]. The Mayo Clinic emphasizes that a rectal, ear, or temporal artery temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher is a true fever [N3-F3].

### 2. **Watch for other symptoms**
Keep notes on the baby’s symptoms, feeding, stool, temperature, and any changes in behavior [N1-F1]. This helps the provider determine whether the fever is mild or part of a more serious illness.

### 3. **Stay hydrated and keep the baby comfortable**
The evidence supports keeping the baby hydrated and using gentle comfort measures [N5-R2][N5-R4]. The Mayo Clinic says to ensure the child is drinking lots of liquids so they stay hydrated [N5-R2]. MedlinePlus notes that fluids help regulate body temperature and replace fluids lost through fever [N5-R4].

### 4. **Avoid giving fever-reducing medicine unless appropriate**
The Mayo Clinic says that for children younger than 3 months, **do not give acetaminophen until the baby has been seen by the healthcare team** [N3-F3]. It also says that for children younger than 6 months, acetaminophen should be used only after age 6 months [N3-F3]. The evidence supports using ibuprofen for children older than 6 months [N3-F3], but only as directed and not automatically.

### 5. **Do not rely on home treatment alone**
The evidence emphasizes that fever may be a sign of a more serious condition in infants, so it is not safe to assume the fever is harmless [N3-F3][N4-R4]. The safest approach is to seek medical advice if the baby is young, the fever is high, or there are any red flags.

---

## 5. When to call 911 or go to the ER

The evidence supports calling 911 or going to the ER for the following situations:

- The baby is **under 3 months old** and has a fever of **100.4°F or higher** [N3-F3][N1-R2].
- The baby has a **very high fever** (above 39°C / 102.2°F) or is **not feeding well, refusing breast or bottle, or too weak to move** [N1-R5].
- The baby has **trouble breathing, grunting, bluish lips, or retractions** [N2-F2].
- The baby has **purple or blood-red spots on the skin** with fever [N2-F2].
- The baby has a **bulging soft spot, stiff neck, or other signs of meningitis** [N2-F2][N4-F4].
- The baby is **lethargic, difficult to wake, or acting abnormally** [N2-F2].

Seattle Children’s also says that if the child has any of the listed symptoms, call the doctor now or go to the nearest ER, and for some symptoms, call 911 [N2-F2]. The evidence is strongest that **young infants with fever should be evaluated urgently**, while older infants are more concerning if fever is associated with other severe symptoms [N3-F3][N1-F1].

---

## 6. How to interpret fever trends and duration

The evidence suggests that fever trends and duration matter, but they are not the only deciding factor.

- For children **6 to 24 months old**, a temperature higher than 101°F that lasts longer than one day may warrant contacting the care team sooner [N3-F3].
- However, the evidence also says that a baby older than 6 months may not need treatment unless clearly uncomfortable [N3-F3]. That means a fever may not be urgent on its own, but it should still be watched carefully if it is persistent or associated with other symptoms.

The evidence is clearest that **fever in babies under 3 months is more concerning than fever in older infants** [N3-F3][N1-F1]. So even a low fever in a very young baby can be a red flag.

---

## 7. Practical advice for parents

### What to do now
- **Check the baby’s temperature carefully** with a reliable thermometer [N5-R1][N3-F3].
- **Record the temperature and any symptoms** so you can share them with the healthcare provider [N1-F1].
- **Keep the baby hydrated** and offer plenty of fluids [N5-R2][N5-R4].
- **Avoid giving acetaminophen to infants younger than 3 months** without medical advice [N3-F3].
- **Do not give fever-reducing medicine automatically**; use it only if the baby is clearly uncomfortable and the provider says it is safe [N5-R3][N5-R5].

### What to avoid
- Do not assume a mild fever means everything is fine, especially in a very young baby [N3-F3][N4-R4].
- Do not delay care if the baby is under 3 months, the fever is high, or there are red flags [N3-F3][N2-F2].
- Do not give more than the recommended dose of acetaminophen [N3-F3].

---

## Final summary

If your baby has a fever, the most important question is **how old the baby is and whether there are any concerning symptoms**. The evidence supports the following rule of thumb:

- **Infants under 3 months**: Fever of 100.4°F or higher is concerning; seek medical evaluation immediately [N3-F3][N1-R2].
- **Babies 3 to 6 months old**: Fever up to 101°F with unusual irritability, lethargy, or discomfort is a reason to contact the care team [N1-F1].
- **Older infants and toddlers**: Fever may be less urgent unless it is very high or associated with red flags such as trouble breathing, stiff neck, poor feeding, or skin rashes [N2-F2][N3-F3].
- **Red flags that require urgent care**: lethargy, difficulty breathing, stiff neck, bulging soft spot, poor feeding, very high fever, or skin rashes with fever [N2-F2][N1-R5].
- **What to do next**: monitor temperature, keep the baby hydrated, and contact the doctor before assuming the fever is harmless [N5-R1][N1-F1][N3-F3].

If you are unsure, the safest choice is to **seek medical care promptly**, especially for very young infants or when there are any warning signs. Fever can be a sign of a serious infection, and early evaluation is the best way to protect your baby [N4-R4][N4-F4][N2-F2].
